beats.narration_text: Privet — this is Liam, in for Bear. Yuqing wants to extend a proven job-sponsorship engine to UX and product design by reweighting its existing signals. I asked Claude what Professor Bear would say. Short version — a weights-profile is the right tool only if the old signals still fit design. They don't. The real risk is a missing signal, not a coefficient.

props.command: What feedback would Professor Bear give Yuqing on extending the Reallocation Engine to UX/Product design with a weights-profile?
output: A weights-profile only works if the old signals still fit.
For design, the real risk is a missing signal — not a coefficient.

beats.narration_text: First, what a weights-profile actually assumes.

Reweighting sounds like the low-risk move — same three signals, just different coefficients for design. And it is the right architecture, but only under one condition: that those existing signals stay valid proxies for design roles and simply need different importance.

props.question: Do the existing signals still fit design roles — or does one need to be built from scratch?
props.commit: commit to an answer before the next beat

beats.narration_text: So the real question forks here. Do the old signals still measure the right thing for design? If yes — reweight, fine. But if a genuinely new risk factor exists for design that the old signals never captured, then reweighting is the wrong tool entirely. You need a new signal, not new coefficients.
And for design, there IS a new risk factor.

For software and data roles, whether the job counts as an H-1B specialty occupation is basically settled. For design, it's contested and role-specific. Under the specialty-occupation rule, a 'UX Designer' staffed with business or marketing grads doesn't survive scrutiny — the same title with HCI and a relevant technical degree does. That's a risk the engine's current roles almost never face.
Here's the diagnostic Bear wants surfaced. Look at the company's actual design team. Degrees in HCI, computer science, formal design — that employer has a defensible petition…

beats.narration_text: …and a team of self-taught designers from varied backgrounds invites scrutiny — an RFE waiting to happen. Same job title, opposite risk. No coefficient on funding or posting activity can see that difference.

beats.narration_text: So the project needs a signal the engine has never had. Ask for this:

props.command: Write a specialty_occupation_defensibility(company, role) signal — from the design team's credential ratio + the job description's specificity — that has no analogue in the current SWE/DS scoring.

beats.narration_text: It approximates the actual test: does this role plausibly require a specific, relevant degree? Team credentials plus posting specificity — rewarding HCI and interaction-design language, penalizing vague 'creativity and communication' framing — returns high, low, or an honest 'mixed, insufficient to confirm.'

props.title: specialty_occupation_defensibility.py

beats.narration_text: And don't let this get absorbed into 'sponsorship history.' That signal measures whether a company HAS sponsored — not whether a DESIGN role there would survive scrutiny. Two different questions. Name defensibility as its own component, or the whole new risk factor quietly disappears.

left.label: HAS SPONSORED
left.note: company track record — a history signal

right.label: WOULD SURVIVE
right.note: would THIS design role pass specialty-occupation scrutiny?

beats.narration_text: Now the three signals she's inheriting.

Don't treat all three as 'just reweight.' SEC Form D funding may need a lag adjustment — design hires trail engineering at a newly funded startup, and get cut first in a downturn. Sponsorship history needs disaggregating by job family. ATS activity needs design base rates — fewer roles, longer cycles, a portfolio step. Three signals, three different treatments.

Sponsorship history is the one most likely to mislead. A company that reliably sponsors engineers tells you little about whether it would sponsor a designer — willingness is role-specific inside a single company. Reweight it naively and a strong engineering record makes a design dead end look green.
beats.pantry_note: Tier 1 illustrative: a company sponsorship 'trophy shelf' full for engineering, empty for design.

beats.narration_text: And there's a quieter problem underneath all of it.

Design-track sponsorship outcomes are a much smaller dataset than the engine's current focus — fewer filings, fewer public RFE outcomes. Tune weights by eyeballing a handful of known-good and known-bad examples and the profile fits those cases, not a pattern. Ask how big the calibration set is, validate on held-out cases, and if it's too thin, say so — don't paper over it with a confident three-color output.
Robustness aimed at exactly this extension.

Four tests. Signal-necessity: remove the new defensibility signal — how often does the classification change? Cross-role stability: run the same company through the general and the design profile — where do they disagree, and is it explainable? Thin-data sensitivity: nudge the weights — do real classifications flip? And a vague-versus-specific posting stress test for the new signal itself.

The posting stress test is the sharp one. Feed the defensibility score a batch of vague listings — 'looking for a creative problem-solver' — against specific ones naming HCI and interaction design. If it doesn't actually separate them, and just returns a middling score for everything, the signal isn't measuring what she thinks it is.

beats.narration_text: Last — what the candidate actually sees.

Surface the defensibility signal as its own visible factor — a designer gains far more from reading 'this company's design team looks credential-mismatched for H-1B purposes' than from a single color that happens to be a little lower. Don't fold the most important new finding into an aggregate.

left.label: AGGREGATE
left.note: defensibility hidden inside composite score — one color, no explanation

right.label: VISIBLE FACTOR
right.note: specialty-occupation defensibility: its own labeled row, legible to the candidate

beats.narration_text: Show the design-specific sponsorship record separately from the company-wide one, so a strong engineering history can't quietly mislead. And flag thin-data confidence — a design-track score built on a small set should read as less certain than the general-track output, even at the same color.

right.label: DESIGN-SPECIFIC
right.note: thin / uncertain — hatched for low confidence

beats.narration_text: Under all of it, one idea: a weights-profile assumes the old signals still fit. For design, one of them doesn't exist yet. That's the difference between reweighting and recognizing a new risk — and it's the move that would make this a real contribution to Bear's engine, not a parameter tweak. Leave Yuqing the open questions: how to source team-credential data at scale, and what to do with a company that has no prior design hires at all.

Let's recap with Claude. Bear's notes for Yuqing, in five. A weights-profile only works if the old signals still fit — for design, specialty-occupation defensibility is a missing signal, not a coefficient. Walk the three inherited signals one by one; they don't all just reweight. The design dataset is thin — validate on held-out cases and say so. Test the extension directly. And show defensibility and design-specific sponsorship as their own visible factors. Well-scoped project — now make it a new signal, not a tweak.

artifactLines: Weights-profile works only if old signals still fit — for design, one doesn't
Specialty-occupation defensibility = a NEW signal, not a coefficient
Walk the 3 inherited signals individually: lag-adjust / disaggregate / re-baserate
Thin design data / validate on held-out; state the limit honestly
Visualize defensibility + design-specific sponsorship as their own factors

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude whenever you're reweighting a model for a new group. It forces you to prove each old signal still fits, catch the new risk factor that needs its own signal, check your data isn't too thin, and find where the picture buries the thing that matters — then it leaves you two open questions. Run it before you call a reweight 'done,' and watch which of your signals it refuses to let you carry over.

props.command: I'm extending a scoring model to a new sub-population by reweighting its existing signals. Pressure-test that plan: (1) for each inherited signal, make me prove it's still a valid proxy for the new group — and flag any genuinely new risk factor that reweighting can't capture and that needs its own signal; (2) find any signal I'm treating as 'just reweight' that actually needs a structural change or disaggregation; (3) ask how thin my calibration data is for the new group and whether I validated on held-out cases; (4) tell me where the visualization hides an important new factor inside an aggregate. End with two open questions I have to answer myself.

beats.narration_text: Claude, Defensible.
